title: Morning Edition
notes: Morning Edition for Monday, Nov 9, 2026. It covers developments since Sunday’s Morning Edition, with ongoing stories marked with their earlier dates.

The lead is House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries backing an impeachment vote on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, expected this week. Top stories: Nvidia’s board probe after reports that Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence, Ottawa’s split of $600 million for film, TV and music, a second performing-arts campus planned in Ta Kwu Ling, China’s October price data, and Gadi Eisenkot formally receiving Israel’s mandate.

The U.S. has five stories; Canada, Hong Kong and World have four; China has three, because fresh, well-sourced China news this weekend was thinner and we did not pad. Culture appears in the U.S. (“Wanted” on Broadway), Canada (screen and music funding), Hong Kong (HKAPA campus) and China (micro-drama rules); sports in the U.S. (Giants), Canada (women’s hockey worlds), Hong Kong (Hong Kong Tennis Open) and World (Paris Masters).
The Hegseth impeachment vote, Eisenkot’s coalition talks and Canada’s next hockey game are described as planned or under way; none had concluded when this edition was compiled.
provenance: Stories are compiled from the linked sources; labels describe the type of claim each story rests on.
Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:24 and 6:27 AM ET; the logged check time (6:26 AM ET) was recorded for the whole research batch rather than per page.

Xinhua and Global Times items are labelled State media. The SCMP article was partly paywalled and only its opening was read; the Globe and Mail article is subscriber content. Two Chinese-government statistics pages timed out in our web fetch but opened by direct download. Politico and Times of Israel pages did not load in our fetch and were not relied on.

Several items rest on a single outlet and are marked so in their source notes. Conflicting figures (Egypt injuries, Gascon’s saves, China egg prices, Miller’s appointment day) are flagged on each story.

stories.headline: Jeffries says he is a “hard yes” on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, with a House vote expected this week
stories.deck: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he backs Republican Rep. Thomas Massie’s push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war.
stories.summary: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he backs Republican Rep. Thomas Massie’s push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said, accusing Hegseth of abusing his power and engineering a “reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.” NBC News reports the resolution is expected to be filed early this week with a vote to follow; the BBC says Massie plans to introduce it as early as Monday. According to the BBC, Massie’s resolution has eight articles alleging Hegseth made war on Iran without the congressional authorisation the 1973 War Powers Resolution requires. Hegseth has called the effort “the politics of personal destruction,” the Pentagon told the BBC he followed the law, and President Trump called the impeachment push “very unfair” in a CBS “60 Minutes” interview. Jeffries said House Democrats would discuss the resolution on Tuesday morning.
stories.why: Even if the House impeaches Hegseth, removal needs a two-thirds Senate vote, so the real test is how many Republicans break ranks — an early measure of how much the Iran war and the midterm losses have loosened the party’s loyalty to Trump’s cabinet.
stories.label: Reported + allegation
stories.note: The impeachment articles are allegations, not findings. The vote had not been held at the time of writing; timing comes from NBC News and the BBC and could change. The current House is still the outgoing one: Democrats take control in January.

stories.headline: Nvidia’s board opens an independent probe after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence
stories.deck: Nvidia’s board said on Sunday it is opening an independent investigation after reports that founder and CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
stories.summary: Nvidia’s board said on Sunday it is opening an independent investigation after reports that founder and CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, with outside counsel, will oversee it; the board said it has “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised and that Huang supports the review. The move follows reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times, cited by CNBC, that U.S. intelligence agencies are concerned that Alice Huang — a businesswoman linked to the Nvidia customer Megaspeed, and no relation to the CEO — has been passing information to Beijing. In an email to staff, Huang said he had an affair with her and apologised to his family. CNBC notes Nvidia reports quarterly earnings on Nov. 17, and three House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to brief them on Nov. 18.
stories.why: Nvidia makes the chips at the heart of the U.S.–China AI race, so any question about its CEO’s exposure to Chinese intelligence lands on export-control policy and investor confidence at once.
stories.label: Official statement + allegation + unnamed sources
stories.note: The spying concerns are reported allegations attributed to U.S. intelligence agencies via The New York Times and Financial Times; Donna Daily did not open those original reports (both are paywalled). Nothing has been proven, and no one has been charged.

stories.headline: Trump says his deportation push was “too tough” and that he would “love to do something” on immigration with Democrats
stories.deck: In a “60 Minutes” interview aired on Sunday, President Trump said his deportation drive may have been “too tough” on long-settled immigrants with jobs and that it hurt him at the polls.
stories.summary: In a “60 Minutes” interview aired on Sunday, President Trump said his deportation drive may have been “too tough” on long-settled immigrants with jobs and that it hurt him at the polls. He said he got “an A+ for closing up the border” but was hurt by removing people who “had good jobs,” and that he would “love to do something on immigration” with Democrats, who control both chambers from January. ABC News reports he floated working out “a deal” for people who have been in the country for 10 to 15 years, without giving terms. CBS notes it is unclear whether enforcement will change: Trump has just named Stephen Miller, an architect of the crackdown, as White House chief of staff. CBS exit polling cited in its report found 58% of voters think the administration’s immigration actions have gone too far.
stories.why: A president conceding his signature policy cost votes opens a door to bargaining with the new Democratic Congress — but with Miller now running the White House, whether enforcement actually softens is the thing to watch.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Trump gave no specifics of any deal. The two sources differ on timing of Miller’s appointment: CBS says Trump replaced Susie Wiles on Friday; ABC says Monday. Donna Daily reported the appointment on Nov. 7.

stories.headline: New Broadway musical “Wanted” opens to mixed reviews that single out its powerhouse singers
stories.deck: “Wanted,” an original musical about two outlaw sisters in 1890s Texas, opened at the James Earl Jones Theatre on Sunday; critics broadly praised the voices but faulted the plotting.
stories.summary: “Wanted,” an original musical about two outlaw sisters in 1890s Texas, opened at the James Earl Jones Theatre on Sunday; critics broadly praised the voices but faulted the plotting. Angelica Chéri wrote the book and lyrics, inspired by a family legend about her great-great-aunts Mary and Martha Clarke, with music by Ross Baum and direction by Stevie Walker-Webb. Solea Pfeiffer and Liisi LaFontaine play the sisters, with R&B singer Ledisi as their mother and Luke James. In BroadwayWorld’s roundup of 14 reviews (average 62.9%), The New York Times called it messy but said “a great musical could yet be somewhere inside,” Variety called the vocal talent “beyond exceptional,” and Deadline said nearly every song builds to the same “roof-raising” belt.
stories.why: Original musicals by Black women writers are still rare on Broadway; whether “Wanted” can survive mixed notices on the strength of its cast will say a lot about how much room the season leaves for new, non-franchise work.
stories.label: Reported + opinion
stories.note: Review quotes are critics’ opinions, collected by BroadwayWorld; Donna Daily did not open each review separately.

stories.headline: Giants win in Philadelphia for the first time since 2013, handing the Eagles a seventh straight loss
stories.deck: Jameis Winston came off the bench for the injured JJ McCarthy and threw the go-ahead touchdown as the New York Giants beat the Eagles 19-11 on Sunday.
stories.summary: Jameis Winston came off the bench for the injured JJ McCarthy and threw the go-ahead touchdown as the New York Giants beat the Eagles 19-11 on Sunday. The 5-2-1 Giants are the only NFC East team with a winning record, and it was their first win in Philadelphia since October 2013 after 13 straight home losses there. The 2-7 Eagles, with Jalen Hurts likely out for the season with blood clots, are on their longest losing run since 2012. Elsewhere in Week 9, the Jets fell 35-12 at Kansas City for their fourth straight loss, and the Bengals beat the Falcons 34-17 at Madrid’s Bernabéu.
stories.why: A first-place Giants team in November changes the mood in New York, while the Eagles’ slide could make them sellers before Tuesday’s trade deadline.

stories.headline: Ottawa sets out how its $600 million for film, TV and music will be split, with the Canada Media Fund getting the most
stories.deck: Culture Minister Marc Miller announced on Sunday how $600 million promised to Canada’s screen and music sectors this fiscal year will flow through six existing funds and agencies.
stories.summary: Culture Minister Marc Miller announced on Sunday how $600 million promised to Canada’s screen and music sectors this fiscal year will flow through six existing funds and agencies. The Globe and Mail reports the Canada Media Fund gets the largest share, $213.4 million, with $68.5 million for Telefilm Canada, $67 million for music through the Canada Music Fund, $51 million for the Indigenous Screen Office, $10 million for Northern Aboriginal Broadcasting and up to $5 million for the Canada History Fund; independent production and local-news funds share $185.1 million. Ottawa says the money is meant to stabilise the sectors while longer-term streaming policy is worked out. The Globe notes the package was first promised in June, after the government asked the CRTC to pause a rule requiring foreign streamers to contribute 15% of Canadian revenue, and that industry groups have warned it is no substitute for enforceable obligations on streamers.
stories.why: For Canadian actors, crews and musicians, this is bridge money: it keeps productions financed this year, but the bigger fight — whether Netflix and other streamers must pay into Canadian content — is still unresolved.
stories.label: Official figures + reported
stories.note: Per-fund amounts are as reported by The Globe and Mail from Canadian Heritage’s backgrounder; the government news release itself lists the six recipients but not the amounts, and the backgrounder was not opened. The Globe article is subscriber content.

stories.headline: B.C. wildfire crews welcome budget money for water bombers but say the people on the ground need help too
stories.deck: Front-line wildland firefighters in British Columbia welcomed the federal budget’s up to $2.5 billion in financing to double water-bomber production, but told CBC News that crews need better support.
stories.summary: Front-line wildland firefighters in British Columbia welcomed the federal budget’s up to $2.5 billion in financing to double water-bomber production, but told CBC News that crews need better support. The Finance Ministry says the money will help De Havilland Canada open a second assembly line in Alberta, raising output of Canadair water bombers to 20 aircraft a year. Firefighters said aircraft can be grounded by wind and smoke, and that weaker benefits than structural firefighters drive high turnover. One Indigenous fire-services director called for funding for prescribed and cultural burns and a national accreditation system for contract crews. B.C. saw 1,474 wildfires burn more than 4,700 square kilometres in 2026, destroying or damaging over 500 structures.
stories.why: Planes are a visible, buildable answer to worsening fire seasons; the crews’ point is that the harder, cheaper fixes — keeping experienced people and burning fuel before summer — are what decide whether towns are saved.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Single outlet. Budget 2026 was tabled on Nov. 5 (first covered in Donna Daily on Nov. 6).

stories.headline: York University says personal data was stolen from departmental web forms used as far back as 2007
stories.deck: Toronto’s York University says an “unauthorized actor” stole personal information submitted through some departmental online forms between 2007 and October 2026.
stories.summary: Toronto’s York University says an “unauthorized actor” stole personal information submitted through some departmental online forms between 2007 and October 2026. The forms were used for things like residence applications, meeting registrations and surveys across 14 university websites, from the Centre for Refugee Studies to the Schulich School of Business. York says most of the stolen data was basic contact details and student ID numbers, but its notice lists categories such as health information, disability status and, for some, sexual orientation. A small number of people whose government ID or financial account details were exposed are being offered two years of credit monitoring. York found the incident on Oct. 25, says its investigation found no sign the intruder reached other systems, and has reported it to police and Ontario’s privacy commissioner.
stories.why: Years-old forms that nobody thinks about are a common weak point; the breach is a reminder for students anywhere that sensitive information handed over for a one-off survey can sit online for decades.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: York has not said how the intrusion happened or how many people were affected.

stories.headline: Canada routs Japan 9-0 at the women’s hockey world championship in Denmark
stories.deck: Nine different Canadians scored as Canada beat Japan 9-0 in Herning, Denmark, on Sunday to go 2-0 at the women’s world championship.
stories.summary: Nine different Canadians scored as Canada beat Japan 9-0 in Herning, Denmark, on Sunday to go 2-0 at the women’s world championship. Nineteen-year-old defender Chloe Primerano opened the scoring, Canada led 4-0 after two periods and added five goals in the third, and goaltender Eve Gascon earned the shutout. Japan’s Riko Kawaguchi made 45 saves, according to the IIHF. Canada, the reigning silver medallists, top Group B and are scheduled to play host Denmark on Monday.
stories.why: With several players scoring their first national-team goals, lopsided group wins let Canada’s coaches test depth before the knockout rounds that decide the medals.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: Sources differ slightly on Gascon’s workload: CBC/The Canadian Press says she stopped all 11 shots; the IIHF says 12 saves.

stories.headline: Government proposes nearly doubling Ta Kwu Ling’s university town, with land set aside for a second HKAPA campus
stories.deck: A Development Bureau paper proposes expanding the campus zone of the planned Ta Kwu Ling university town from 40 to 75 hectares, reserving about seven hectares for a second campus of the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts.
stories.summary: A Development Bureau paper proposes expanding the campus zone of the planned Ta Kwu Ling university town from 40 to 75 hectares, reserving about seven hectares for a second campus of the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts. According to the paper, submitted to the North District Council and reported by The Standard and the SCMP, the campus zone would span 10 sites along the Ping Yuen and Shenzhen rivers, with shared libraries, sports grounds, labs and dormitories. The wider priority development area near Heung Yuen Wai would grow 20% to 250 hectares, with about 13,000 homes and 27,000 jobs. Land resumption is expected from the second quarter of 2028, with the first plots ready by 2030 at the earliest.
stories.why: HKAPA is the city’s only public performing-arts school, and a second campus in the Northern Metropolis would be a long-term bet that drama, dance and film training can grow alongside the border tech hub — though the timetable runs into the 2030s.
stories.label: Reported + official proposal
stories.note: This is a proposal in a government paper, not an approved plan. The SCMP article is partly paywalled; only its opening was read.

stories.headline: About 40 visitors stranded when Ocean Park’s observation tower stalls near the top
stories.deck: Around 40 people were stuck on Ocean Park Tower’s rotating cabin on Monday afternoon Hong Kong time after the ride malfunctioned and stopped near the top.
stories.summary: Around 40 people were stuck on Ocean Park Tower’s rotating cabin on Monday afternoon Hong Kong time after the ride malfunctioned and stopped near the top. Police and fire services were alerted at about 3:30 p.m.; park staff led most passengers down a backup stairwell, and a firefighter brought down one visitor who felt unwell by rope. The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department says it will investigate and has required the park to submit an incident report. The same ride stalled in May 2025, stranding riders for nearly two hours after its safety system was triggered.
stories.why: A second breakdown in about 18 months at one of the city’s best-known attractions puts pressure on Ocean Park and regulators to explain what went wrong before tourists lose confidence in the ride.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Monday afternoon in Hong Kong was early Monday morning in New York. The cause had not been given.

stories.headline: Cold front brings Hong Kong’s coolest morning of the autumn, with 16°C forecast for Tuesday
stories.deck: The Observatory recorded 23.2°C on Monday morning, the lowest so far this autumn, and forecasts about 16°C in urban areas on Tuesday morning.
stories.summary: The Observatory recorded 23.2°C on Monday morning, the lowest so far this autumn, and forecasts about 16°C in urban areas on Tuesday morning. An intense northeast monsoon linked to a cold front is affecting the Guangdong coast, bringing fine, dry weather with fresh northerly winds, strong offshore. The New Territories are expected to be a couple of degrees cooler and still “rather cool” on Wednesday morning, with a large day-night temperature range before temperatures rise later in the week.

stories.headline: China’s factory-gate prices rise 5.7% on energy costs while consumer inflation stays at 0.7%
stories.deck: China’s producer price index rose 5.7% from a year earlier in October, up from 5% in September, while consumer prices rose 0.7%, official data released on Monday show.
stories.summary: China’s producer price index rose 5.7% from a year earlier in October, up from 5% in September, while consumer prices rose 0.7%, official data released on Monday show. The National Bureau of Statistics says mining prices jumped 27.9% and input prices paid by manufacturers rose 7.9%. Consumer prices were flat from September: food fell 2.9% year on year, led by a 16.9% drop in fresh vegetables and an 8.6% fall in pork, while non-food prices rose 1.5%. State news agency Xinhua quotes an NBS statistician attributing the moves to imported inflation and domestic demand, with gasoline up 22.4% and AI-driven demand lifting prices of data-storage equipment, tablets, computers and phones.
stories.why: Rising factory-gate prices end years of deflation pressure for Chinese industry, but if energy costs keep feeding through while consumer demand stays weak, manufacturers’ margins — and the prices of Chinese goods abroad — will be squeezed.
stories.label: Official figures + state media
stories.note: Figures are official NBS data. Xinhua (state media) reports egg prices up 12.3% year on year; the NBS release says 10.1%. Explanations for the price moves come from officials.

stories.headline: Fire in a Taiyuan high-rise kills five as trapped people break windows to call for help
stories.deck: A fire in a high-rise building in Taiyuan, capital of Shanxi province, killed five people on Sunday afternoon; 38 people were taken to hospital in total, according to local authorities.
stories.summary: A fire in a high-rise building in Taiyuan, capital of Shanxi province, killed five people on Sunday afternoon; 38 people were taken to hospital in total, according to local authorities. The district government said the fire broke out at 4:59 p.m. local time on Liuxiang South Road in Yingze District and was put out by 7 p.m. Local emergency officials said the first to third floors mostly housed training businesses, the fifth to seventh were vacant and the eighth and ninth held a hotel. Videos showed several floors ablaze with people at the windows calling for help. The cause is under investigation.
stories.why: Fires in mixed-use buildings packed with tutoring centres and small hotels have been a recurring killer in Chinese cities, and investigators will look at whether exits and fire-safety rules were followed.

stories.headline: China’s broadcast regulator launches a two-month crackdown on vulgar and copycat AI micro-dramas
stories.deck: The National Radio and Television Administration has begun a two-month campaign, running from Nov. 1 to the end of December, against low-quality and look-alike micro-dramas, focusing on AI-made content.
stories.summary: The National Radio and Television Administration has begun a two-month campaign, running from Nov. 1 to the end of December, against low-quality and look-alike micro-dramas, focusing on AI-made content. Its notice targets content harmful to children, borderline sexual material, extreme conflict, money worship and plots that flout family ethics, as well as AI “face-stealing” and “voice-stealing.” Platforms are also told to stop re-airing the same series under new titles or character names and to diversify homepage and chart recommendations. The regulator says 75,000 micro-dramas have been taken down and more than 1,500 accounts dealt with so far this year.
stories.why: Micro-dramas — minute-long vertical episodes — are one of China’s fastest-growing entertainment businesses, and the rules written for AI-generated actors and voices there are likely to shape how the format develops elsewhere.
stories.label: Official statement
stories.note: Based on the regulator’s own Chinese-language notice; Aju Press’s English report cites Xinhua and Yonhap. Enforcement results will come from the regulator itself.

stories.headline: Eisenkot formally receives the mandate to form Israel’s government and calls for a “national emergency government”
stories.deck: Israel’s President Isaac Herzog formally handed Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government on Sunday, giving him 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.
stories.summary: Israel’s President Isaac Herzog formally handed Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government on Sunday, giving him 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. At the ceremony Eisenkot said Israel was “approaching a point of no return” and that “creative and unconventional” steps would be needed to form a “national emergency government”; he invited Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud and the Religious Zionist Party to join on his terms. Eisenkot received 67 recommendations in consultations to Netanyahu’s 46, including backing from both Arab-led parties, though that does not commit them to join. No bloc won a 61-seat majority in the Oct. 27 election, and the Jerusalem Post notes that failure could lead to a unity government, a minority government or another election.
stories.why: Eisenkot has the first shot but no ready majority; whether he can bridge ultra-Orthodox and Arab parties — or lure parts of Netanyahu’s camp — will decide if Israel gets a new government or heads back to the polls.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Ongoing story: Donna Daily reported Eisenkot’s 67 recommendations on Nov. 6 and Herzog’s choice on Nov. 8; the formal ceremony, then scheduled, took place on Sunday.

stories.headline: Winter storm floods Gaza’s tent camps as the UN says stocks of tents and tarpaulins inside are nearly gone
stories.deck: Heavy rain and strong winds from Nov. 6 flooded displacement sites across Gaza, and the UN says emergency stocks of tents, tarpaulins and blankets inside the territory are virtually exhausted.
stories.summary: Heavy rain and strong winds from Nov. 6 flooded displacement sites across Gaza, and the UN says emergency stocks of tents, tarpaulins and blankets inside the territory are virtually exhausted. The UN humanitarian office (OCHA) says more than 26,000 households had appealed for help by Nov. 8 and that an infant reportedly drowned; Gaza’s Civil Defense said a sand hill collapsed onto tents near Deir al-Balah, killing five people, including three children. The Hamas-run government media office put the number of flooded tents at about 70,000. OCHA says more than 150,000 tents are waiting outside Gaza and that more Israeli approvals and funding are urgently needed; Israel says it restricts items that could be used for military purposes.
stories.why: About 1.4 million people in Gaza live in tents or makeshift shelters, so the first storm of winter is a preview of months of cold and flooding unless supplies get in faster.
stories.label: Reported + official figures
stories.note: Figures measure different things and are preliminary: 70,000 flooded tents is the Hamas-run government’s count; OCHA counts 26,000+ household appeals. The deaths were reported by Gaza’s Civil Defense and relayed by OCHA.

stories.headline: Two passenger trains collide south of Cairo, killing at least seven people
stories.deck: A train heading from Giza to Fayoum rear-ended another bound for Aswan about 76 km south of Cairo on Sunday, killing at least seven people and injuring more than 100, Egyptian authorities said.
stories.summary: A train heading from Giza to Fayoum rear-ended another bound for Aswan about 76 km south of Cairo on Sunday, killing at least seven people and injuring more than 100, Egyptian authorities said. Several carriages derailed or overturned. The dead include the driver of the Fayoum-bound train, according to a government statement reported by The National, which says the Aswan train had made an unscheduled stop. President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi ordered a swift investigation and said anyone found negligent would be held accountable; prosecutors are investigating the technical cause.
stories.why: Egypt has borrowed heavily to modernise one of the region’s oldest rail networks, and another deadly collision will raise questions about signalling and safety on the busy line to Upper Egypt.

stories.headline: Alcaraz beats Ben Shelton to win the Paris Masters for the first time
stories.deck: Carlos Alcaraz beat American Ben Shelton 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 in Sunday’s Paris Masters final, his first title at the event in six attempts and his ninth Masters 1000 crown.
stories.summary: Carlos Alcaraz beat American Ben Shelton 7-6 (7-5), 7-5 in Sunday’s Paris Masters final, his first title at the event in six attempts and his ninth Masters 1000 crown. The win avenged his US Open quarter-final loss to Shelton in September, which came on his return from a four-month wrist injury; the BBC says he has since won three titles and lost once in 17 matches. Alcaraz saved all six break points he faced in the first set and came back from a break down in the second. He is the first Spaniard to win the event since David Ferrer in 2012, according to Reuters via The Guardian, and heads to the ATP Finals in Turin on a nine-match winning streak.
stories.why: Back-to-back titles in Vienna and Paris confirm Alcaraz is fully fit again and set up a rivalry with Shelton that could define the men’s game in 2027.

stories.note: Ongoing story: Donna Daily reported the final as scheduled on Nov. 8; this reports the result.
